items.title: Trainable sparse dendritic networks reveal regime-dependent roles for shunting inhibition and morphology
items.subtitle: ARXIV · Q-BIO.NC · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Houman Safaai, Maceo Richards, Ryan Whalen, Adithya Madduri, Naeem Khoshnevis, Bernardo L. Sabatini
items.summary: arXiv:2611.17434v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Neural circuits must compute reliably despite noise and changes in context. We introduce DendriNet, a framework for training scalable rate-based networks with sparse excitatory and inhibitory contacts, controllable dendritic architecture and different synaptic integration rules. In image classification, shunting networks transmit and rely on distal dendritic signals more strongly than additive networks. Distributing limited contacts across compartments improves classification in small populations, whereas greater serial dendritic depth offers no clean-image benefit in resource-matched trees. Robustness depends on the perturbation. Deeper shunting trees better tolerate independent pixel noise, whereas additive trees better tolerate strong input scaling. On a contextual task with gain variation and noise, the primary shunting tree is more accurate than the separately tuned additive tree under the noise and gain conditions used during training, yet depends less on cue-specific inhibition. Learning dendritic leak conductances partly restores shunting accuracy on dim, noise-free inputs outside the training distribution. At AlexNet width, shunting integration and learned sparse connectivity support smaller deployed networks with accuracy comparable to the retrained dense layers they replace. These results relate dendritic organization and synaptic integration to noise tolerance and contextual computation, and suggest tests of dendritic function and design principles for brain-inspired networks.

items.title: Subjective functions
items.subtitle: ARXIV · Q-BIO.NC · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Samuel J. Gershman
items.summary: arXiv:2512.15948v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Where do objective functions come from? How do we select what goals to pursue? Human intelligence is adept at synthesizing new objective functions on the fly. How does this work, and can we endow artificial systems with the same ability? This paper proposes an approach to answering these questions, starting with the concept of a subjective function, a higher-order objective function that is endogenous to the agent (i.e., defined with respect to the agent's features, rather than an external task). Expected prediction error is studied as a concrete example of a subjective function. This proposal has many connections to ideas in psychology, neuroscience, and machine learning.

items.title: From Clever Hans to Hypotheses: Interpreting EEG Foundational Transformers with LRP
items.subtitle: ARXIV · Q-BIO.NC · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Justus Meyer zu Bexten, Nico Scherf, Bogdan Franczyk, Simon M. Hofmann
items.summary: arXiv:2605.11885v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Emerging foundation models (FMs) in electroencephalography (EEG) promise a path to scale deep learning in diagnostics and brain-computer interfaces despite data scarcity, yet their opaque nature remains a barrier to wider adoption. We investigate attention-aware Layer-wise relevance propagation (LRP) as a post-hoc attribution method for EEG-FMs, extending LRP's use on convolutional neural network (CNN)-based EEG models to the Transformer architectures that current FMs are based on. We find that LRP can both verify EEG-FM decisions and surface novel, biologically plausible hypotheses from them. In motor imagery, it unmasks 'Clever Hans' behavior where models prioritize task correlated ocular signals over the intended motor correlates. In a naturalistic paradigm for affect prediction, it reveals a recurring reliance on a central electrode cluster, suggesting a candidate sensorimotor signature of arousal. Though heatmap interpretation remains ambiguous in this complex domain, the results position LRP as a tool for both verification and exploration of EEG-FMs, a role that will grow in both importance and discovery potential as the underlying models mature.

items.title: From Organization to Viability: A Multi-Level Analysis of Gait Dynamics Under Occlusal Constraint
items.subtitle: ARXIV · Q-BIO.NC · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Jacques Raynal, Pierre Slangen, Elsa Raynal, Jacques Margerit
items.summary: arXiv:2605.13893v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Clinical interpretation often assumes that observable performance sufficiently reflects the organization of an adaptive system. The preceding Level 3 study showed that neither an aggregated scalar score nor a static exploratory UMAP embedding uniquely resolved the occlusal observational probes. This study introduces Level 4, centered on observed longitudinal viability. Using an exploratory single-case design in a participant with Parkinson's disease, gait was recorded with instrumented insoles under three probes: neutral natural occlusion (ONL), a nominal 2.5-degree increase in vertical dimension of occlusion (OC2.5), and a nominal 3-degree increase (OC3). Two sessions were conducted eleven weeks apart. A common PCA representation was used to compare M1-M2 centroid displacement. In the selected PC1-PC2 plane, OC3 showed the smallest Euclidean displacement, ONL an intermediate displacement, and OC2.5 the largest. This ordering was preserved in most bootstrap iterations but was not preserved after Mahalanobis covariance normalization, showing that within-condition dispersion contributes to the result. Level 4 therefore provides a retrospective, representation-dependent proxy for longitudinal reorganization when static representations remain non-identifying. The findings are exploratory and non-causal. They do not establish distinct physiological states, a causal occlusal effect, a validated viability threshold, a therapeutic optimum, or a covariance-independent ranking.

items.title: EEG-FM-Audit: A Systematic Evaluation and Analysis Pipeline for EEG Foundation Models
items.subtitle: ARXIV · Q-BIO.NC · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Xianheng Wang, Yige Yang, Damien Coyle
items.summary: arXiv:2605.26910v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: EEG foundation models (EEG-FMs) show potential for learning generalized representations from heterogeneous EEG signals. However, existing studies exhibit three critical limitations: opaque model tuning, unverified contributions of complex learning paradigms to EEG-FMs, and a limited understanding of the neurophysiological features that FMs rely on to make decisions. To address these challenges, we propose EEG-FM-Audit, a systematic evaluation and diagnostic pipeline comprising three modules: (1) a fairness-calibrated benchmarking protocol ensuring fair comparisons through model-tailored hyperparameter optimization for EEG-FMs and supervised baselines; (2) three paradigm-level ablation workflows isolating contributions of heterogeneous data scale, self-supervised pretraining, and pretrained linguistic priors; and (3) a neurophysiological probing (NPP) framework exploring whether FMs leverage valid EEG features. Extensive experiments across four leading EEG-FMs and five supervised models on four datasets reveal that well-tuned supervised baselines can match or outperform tuned FMs in some cases, despite requiring significantly fewer parameters. Furthermore, ablation analysis indicates that FM pre-training is indispensable for data-scarce downstream tasks, whereas the contribution of pre-trained linguistic components depends heavily on model architecture. Finally, NPP analysis shows that FMs generally extract the established temporal, spatial, and spectral characteristics of the evaluated datasets, establishing a systematic diagnostic benchmark for assessing EEG-FMs.

items.title: Do VLMs Align Better with Humans than LLMs Do during Natural Reading?
items.subtitle: ARXIV · Q-BIO.NC · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Jinzhou Wu, Zhengwu Ma, Jixing Li, Baoping Tang, Zitong Lu
items.summary: arXiv:2605.28818v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have become increasingly useful computational models of human language processing, yet it remains open whether vision--language learning is associated with more human-like text representations during natural reading. We address this question by comparing matched LLM and vision--language model (VLM) pairs under strictly text-only input and evaluating alignment with human brain activity (whole-cortex fMRI) and reading behavior (synchronized regressive saccades). Across evaluated pairs, we identify a selective, rather than global, pattern in human--model alignment. In first-party continued-pretraining pairs (Qwen2 and DeepSeek), VLMs more accurately predicted human regressive saccades while exhibiting practical equivalence with matched LLMs in whole-cortex fMRI alignment, whereas a LoRA-adapted pair (Mistral/Idefics2) showed no divergence. However, sentence-level fMRI analyses revealed a growing VLM advantage for more visually evocative sentences. Together, these findings provide a controlled comparison of matched LLMs and VLMs, showing selective human-alignment advantages in reading behavior and visually grounded content.

items.title: Boosting Brain-to-Image Decoding with TRIBE v2 Data Augmentation
items.subtitle: ARXIV · Q-BIO.NC · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Yohann Benchetrit, Marl\`ene Careil, Simon Dahan, Hubert Banville, St\'ephane d'Ascoli, Jean-R\'emi King
items.summary: arXiv:2606.06345v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Brain decoding is limited by the availability of labeled neural data, and remains challenging in low-data regimes. To address this issue, we investigate whether and when brain decoding can be boosted by augmenting small fMRI datasets with synthetic data generated by a pretrained model of fMRI responses to stimuli. We use TRIBE v2, a large encoding model pretrained on more than 1000 hours of fMRI responses to video, audio and language. For each dataset, we evaluate systematic grids that show how the performance of image decoders varies with the amount of synthetic data used for training. Our results, based on two datasets (the 7T fMRI Natural Scenes Dataset and 3T fMRI BOLD5000), show up to 68% improvement in Top-10 image-retrieval accuracy compared to decoders trained only on real data. Importantly, the proportion of augmented data required to reach a given image decoding performance needs to be adjusted depending on the data source. Surprisingly, image decoders trained exclusively on synthetic fMRI can perform above chance in some settings, suggesting that TRIBE v2 can support zero-shot brain-to-image decoding. Together, these results show how large-scale models of the fMRI responses to sight, sound and language may provide a foundation to improve the data efficiency for image decoding.

items.title: NeuroLens: Learning Latent Embeddings of Neural Semantics from Chronic Recordings
items.subtitle: ARXIV · Q-BIO.NC · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Hanrui Lyu, Baiyuan Chen, Tianshu Tan, Matthew R. Whiteway, Maxwell D. Melin, Ji Xia, Linyang He, Bradly C. Stadie, Anne Churchland, Liam Paninski, Yizi Zhang
items.summary: arXiv:2610.02864v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Understanding how neural activity represents higher-order cognition and how these representations evolve during learning is a central pursuit in neuroscience. However, tracking meaningful representational changes remains challenging because recorded neural populations change across days. Here, we introduce NeuroLens (Latent Embeddings of Neural Semantics), a self-supervised model based on the Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (LeJEPA). An adaptive encoder maps changing neural populations into a common latent space, where a temporal predictor forecasts future latent states. Across mouse and human intracortical recordings, NeuroLens learns representations that improve decoding of abstract variables, including decisions and sentence meaning. In chronic mouse neural recordings during visual decision-making, these representations capture gradual transitions between learning stages and the progressive orthogonalization of neural states associated with different choices. They also reveal distinct timescales of cortical reorganization across tasks during learning. With multi-day pretraining, these representations also support stable decoding across days, including leading performance on the FALCON benchmark. Together, these findings support NeuroLens as a framework for tracking learning-related representational changes while maintaining stable decoding over long timescales.

items.title: Learning Trajectories Leave Decodable Traces in Neural Network Weight Space and Internal Representations
items.subtitle: ARXIV · Q-BIO.NC · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Patrick Krauss, Achim Schilling, Andreas Maier, Thomas Kinfe, Claus Metzner
items.summary: arXiv:2611.24782v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Neural networks trained on the same task develop related weight-space structures, yet remain distinguishable after learning. Do these differences merely reflect alternative solutions, or do they preserve information about individual learning histories? We tested whether final weights reveal initialization, task order, and earlier trajectory states. Training reorganized the ensemble: initial pairwise distances did not consistently predict final distances. Nevertheless, all 30 trained networks were correctly matched to their initial weights among ten candidates per dataset. Networks sharing an initialization also developed recognizable final hidden representations across different batch schedules, although direct comparisons with initial activity did not recover identity. Learning order remained readable as well. A linear probe decoded the order of two earlier tasks with 100% accuracy on 80 held-out networks after ten epochs of a common final task. Earlier intermediate weight states were partly predictable, but individual initial weights could not be reliably reconstructed. Final weights thus retain selective historical information rather than a complete trajectory record. Perturbed networks recovered classification performance without returning to their unperturbed training paths. This separation persisted across datasets, intervention times, and network layers. Moreover, 2,157 of 2,160 aligned endpoint pairs showed no positive loss barrier at sampled interpolation points, indicating low-loss connections between distinct solutions rather than convergence to one weight vector. Together, these findings show that a shared task constrains networks to related successful solutions without erasing their individual histories. Final weights reflect not only what a network has learned, but also where learning began and how it unfolded.

items.title: Old Matches, New Frames: Schedule-Gated Stereo Memory from Human Vision to Machine Matching
items.subtitle: ARXIV · Q-BIO.NC · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Ruiqi Liu, Yang Lu, Yanlan Kang
items.summary: arXiv:2611.24848v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Human vision and video stereo networks both reuse disparity evidence across time, yet a refresh of the input can invalidate a match formed milliseconds earlier. What tells a system whether an old match still counts? We answer this from limited human data in three steps. First, nine temporal mechanisms share a frozen binocular-energy front end and an equal-capacity readout, so held-out behavior isolates the temporal selection rule: on 240 conditions from 10 observers, down-weighting aged evidence that has lost binocular support lowers subject RMSE from 12.6% to 10.3% and reproduces a period-dependent reversed-depth illusion, across all 59 readings of the unpublished protocol and 8 front-end perturbations. Second, four propositions establish what such data can identify: gating is identified at the level of the refresh schedule, and candidate binding is invisible to standard stimuli but exposed by a single-eye geometry flip that separates the readouts by up to 7.1%. Third, the identified rule becomes a two-field stereo memory that separates sample validity from hypothesis support. It removes a 50 ms recovery lag after geometry flips, and its regime analysis explains why plain integration stays preferable on MPI-Sintel, where 71.1% of pixels change appearance but not disparity.

items.title: From local competition to bump attractors:how excitation width sets capacity, interference and updating in recurrent models of visual working memory
items.subtitle: ARXIV · Q-BIO.NC · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Purvikalyani Prasannah, Rakesh Sengupta
items.summary: arXiv:2611.28601v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: On-centre off-surround (OCOS) networks and bump attractors, the two main recurrent models of visual working memory, differ chiefly in how far recurrent excitation spreads. We place them in one family parameterised by excitation width at fixed total excitation, and ask how stable each stored item is and what it costs the circuit to hold and change it. The answer is that excitation width sets the price of continuity. In the OCOS limit, which we solve exactly by completing the energy-function formalism of \citet{Sengupta2024}, an item occupies a single unit, relaxes quickly and never drifts, and capacity follows in closed form, exact over all stable states. As excitation widens towards a bump-like regime, items become continuous but costly: per item, the circuit uses 15--29 units instead of one and 6.5--11 times the activity, relaxes 35--60 times more slowly after a perturbation, needs a 35--230 times stronger cue to accept a second item, and holds 7--10 items instead of at least 40. Under noise, with background false alarms approximately matched, about a third of wide items drift, whereas narrow items never move. Yet even as an item's translation mode softens towards zero, items remain locked to the lattice. Locking is poorly predicted by energy differences between item positions, but strongly predicted by how far the unit just beyond an item's edge sits below threshold (rank correlation 0.91 across 40 parameter settings). Where that margin vanishes, a new input captures the stored item instead of being added to memory.

items.title: History-bearing thalamocortical signals reconstruct and redirect later decisions in a circuit model
items.subtitle: ARXIV · Q-BIO.NC · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Yanzhe Zhao, Yongzhang Ji
items.summary: arXiv:2611.28799v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Experience can guide an ambiguous choice or bias a choice despite strong current evidence. We asked how a thalamocortical circuit carries historical content forward and regulates its influence across successive decisions. In published data from adult male mice, suppressing posterior parietal cortex (PPC) or pulvinar (PUL) improved current judgments most when sensory history conflicted with the stimulus, reflecting reduced historical weighting. In trained thalamocortical circuit models, replaying recorded PUL input to PPC reconstructed a historical trace after equalizing complete recipient states across histories. Replaying the opposite history redirected the later choice, even after the circuit correctly judged an intervening strong stimulus. This historical message occupied a low-dimensional direction in thalamic output that remained broadly reachable under firing-rate bounds; redistributing the arriving current at matched energy showed that fine spatial organization, beyond total input strength, selectively shapes later history use without disrupting current choices. Strong sensory evidence suppressed historical output while preserving internal state differences, whereas ambiguity recruited neuronal rectification thresholds and readout alignment to express history. Small shifts in the cortical operating point modulated later historical influence, and partial attenuation of recurrent drive reduced it across all circuits while preserving current commitments; correspondingly, recurrent dynamics were essential for predicting post-stimulus trajectories in held-out histories. Together, these findings distinguish three operations in history-guided choice: returning thalamocortical input determines which past is reconstructed, recurrent dynamics carry its influence forward across intervening demands, and current sensory evidence gates how strongly it enters the decision.

items.title: Topological Neural Collapse
items.subtitle: ARXIV · Q-BIO.NC · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Nicholas Enbar-Salo, Jeova Farias Sales Rocha Neto
items.summary: arXiv:2611.28894v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Neural collapse (NC) predicts that, late in training, last-layer class features concentrate at their means and the means form a simplex equiangular tight frame (ETF). We ask whether NC also leaves a signature in the functional connectome of each layer: the graph of Pearson correlations between hidden-unit activations, built per class and summarized by persistent graph homology. items.title: MAS-BIT: A Multi-Agent System for End-to-End BraIn-to-Text Decoding
items.subtitle: ARXIV · Q-BIO.NC · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Xinjie Zhang, Linyang He, Yizi Zhang, Yuesheng Ma, Nima Mesgarani
items.summary: arXiv:2611.29457v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Speech brain-computer interfaces aim to restore communication by translating neural activity into text, yet end-to-end decoders have historically trailed cascaded systems in accuracy. MAS-BIT coordinates three specialized agents: a neural agent that interprets continuous neural representations, a phonetic agent that decodes soft phoneme posteriors, and an arbitration agent that integrates their complementary evidence with direct access to neural representations to generate the final transcription. items.title: Motoric signatures to detect original authorship versus cognitive effort in instructed motor responses of an emerging speaker with ASD
items.subtitle: ARXIV · Q-BIO.NC · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Elizabeth B. Torres
items.summary: arXiv:2611.29594v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: There is at present no objective, agnostic method to track levels of message authorship and agency in non-speakers who rely on assisted typing to communicate. Part of the problem is that nuances in spontaneous gestural movements of the typer transpire largely beneath awareness of both the typer and the communication-regulation-partner. Such spontaneous movements co-occur with the intentional ones producing the typed messages but are currently not considered part of the communication system. We introduce an assay that probes various levels of cognitive loads in an ecologically valid environment. Then, in collaboration with an emerging speaker-typer and his communication-regulation-partner, we empirically estimate motoric stochastic signatures during both independent and assisted typing. Under varying levels of cognitive loads, the assay and biometrics distinguish motoric patterns in spontaneous typing of phrases in response to open-ended questions from those in instructed typing of the same phrase. The non-dominant bodily motions, co-occurring with the dominant (typing) side reveal not only levels of cognitive mental effort and agency of the typer but also levels of creative thoughts through motoric preambles present only in open-ended mode. This level of semantic authorship is detectable in both the geodesic paths along the manifold representing the Gamma stochastic parameters of the motions fluctuations and those of the physical 3D spatial trajectories. The head and facial micro-motions capture these non-dominant-body nuances, offering a personalized motoric metric of cognitive effort, agency, authorship and a comprehensive suite of assays to open new research avenues for assisted typing with haptic support.

items.title: Active sensing as control over sensory acquisition
items.subtitle: ARXIV · Q-BIO.NC · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Neeli Tummala, Mitra J. Hartmann
items.summary: arXiv:2611.29886v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The term "active sensing" is used across neuroscience and engineering to describe a wide range of sensing behaviors, but there is no consensus on what makes sensing "active." We propose that the behaviors grouped under this label are better understood as forms of control over sensory acquisition and develop a framework that distinguishes three interacting forms of control. Mechanistic control physically structures sensory input, strategic control modulates sensing in closed loop through adaptive and attentional processes, and agentic control concerns the sensing policies available to an agent and its authority to choose among them. These forms of control can occur separately or in combination, and have distinct consequences for sensory input, perception, behavior, and performance. The framework clarifies active-passive comparisons and provides a common basis for analyzing biological, engineered, and hybrid sensing systems by asking what is controlled, how, and by whom.

items.title: High-Resolution 3D Micro-CT Database of Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS) Coils for More Accurate Modelling, Technology Benchmarking, and Progress in Coil Design
items.subtitle: ARXIV · Q-BIO.NC · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Maryam Farahmandrad, Max Koehler, Mahdi Bayati, Denis Goldnik, Sergiy Antonyuk, Stephan Goetz
items.summary: arXiv:2611.29051v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Accurate modelling of transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) coils requires coil-specific geometric and electrical parameters. Yet detailed manufacturer models are rarely available, and internals may be widely available to companies in the field but not to researchers. The development of new coils should ideally build on all existing prior art. This work presents a technology benchmark and modelling-ready dataset for seventeen widely used commercial TMS coils across multiple manufacturers and geometries. High-resolution micro-CT (0.0495 mm resolution, material and density contrast) serves to reconstruct winding and casing structures and to extract parameters directly usable in numerical models, including loop dimensions, conductor cross-section, turn count, winding height, and winding-to-surface (casing) thickness. Complementary electrical measurements provide spectral impedance (series resistance and inductance) scans from 20 Hz to 200 kHz, together with dc resistance. In addition to baseline geometry and impedance, the study documents practical construction features relevant to safety and usability with detailed insights into their internal construction (e.g., cooling architectures and embedded sensing). The resulting benchmark dataset supports coil-specific electric-field simulations, reduces modelling uncertainty associated with generic assumptions (e.g., fixed coil-scalp spacing), and provides a quantitative reference for designing and evaluating new coil technologies against established commercial solutions. As a simulation-readiness example, we generated a calibrated CT-derived MCB70 line-current model for SimNIBS and evaluated its effect on predicted electric-field metrics. Compared with the SimNIBS MCB70 model, the CT-derived model produced measurable differences under identical placement conditions. We provide the dataset online.

items.title: Denoised but Not Improved: What EEG Denoising Does to a Downstream Task
items.subtitle: ARXIV · Q-BIO.NC · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Xianglong Bao, Zhe Wang, Kewen Wang, Ming Jin
items.summary: arXiv:2611.29256v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Scalp electroencephalography (EEG) is routinely denoised before it reaches a downstream model, and the denoising literature scores a method by how closely its output matches a clean reference waveform. That reference does not exist for real scalp recordings: it is synthesized by adding artifact templates to signals merely presumed clean, and even an exact separation would return cortical activity blurred by volume conduction rather than the activity itself. Fidelity to it is therefore an unvalidatable objective, and whether it predicts any downstream benefit has gone largely unexamined. We report an audit that examines it. Holding a seizure-detection pipeline fixed and varying only the preprocessing stage, we find that five standard denoising methods, spanning analytic, cross-channel and supervised deep families, all fail to improve on the unprocessed signal, and most degrade it. To say what such a stage must instead do, we formalize a label-only, classifier-free probe that reads it by the separability geometry it induces on task-relevant features, decomposing any change into a between-class distance and a within-class scatter term. On a transform that does improve the task, the probe attributes the entire gain to a roughly one-quarter reduction of within-class scatter, with class separation statistically unchanged. What a downstream model benefits from is therefore variance suppression on task-relevant structure, which waveform-fidelity metrics neither measure nor reward.

items.title: Second-Order Dynamics in Noisy RNNs Produce Exploration and Temporal Compression in Replay
items.subtitle: ARXIV · Q-BIO.NC · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Josue Casco-Rodriguez, Nanda H. Krishna, Richard G. Baraniuk
items.summary: arXiv:2611.29888v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Biological neural networks (like the hippocampus) can internally generate "replay" resembling stimulus-driven activity. Recent computational models of replay use noisy recurrent neural networks (RNNs) trained to path-integrate. Replay in these networks is described as Langevin sampling, but this theory alone fails to capture the environmental exploration and temporal compression observed in real biological replay. To close this gap, we re-examine spontaneous noisy RNN activity ("replay") as Langevin sampling, one timestep at a time, from a time-series distribution resembling lived experiences (unlike previous works which defined sampling as Monte Carlo inference over a static distribution). We provide a normative second-order Langevin sampling framework wherein spike-frequency adaptation drives spatial exploration at the cost of speed, and momentum via dendritic input differentiation drives temporal compression. We numerically verify our framework via simulations of noisy RNNs trained on 2D triangular and T-maze navigation activity, and others trained on place cell activity of synthetic rats. Crucially, we observe that simultaneous adaptation and momentum increases both replay exploration and speed, and provide one of the first accounts for biologically plausible temporal compression in rate-based RNN replay. Our findings encourage experiments into whether dendritic input differentiation, or other mechanisms, may support temporal compression in memory circuits like the hippocampus.

items.title: From joint attention to shared symbols: A free-energy principle account
items.subtitle: ARXIV · Q-BIO.NC · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Tadahiro Taniguchi, Koji Hashimoto, Ryuichiro Ishikawa
items.summary: arXiv:2611.30788v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Joint attention precedes vocabulary acquisition. How can attending to the same object help two people with different sensory experiences come to use a shared word? In a free-energy principle account, marginalizing the common object induces a statistical dependence between private perceptual states. In a categorical world, the joint prior inherits a mixture structure whose component index provides a candidate for shared reference. The collective predictive coding model approximates this prior by representing the dependence through that shared index. An established Metropolis-Hastings naming game lets agents infer and exchange words using private evidence. Toy and multiview image experiments illustrate how word exchange can coordinate private categories and improve the fit of collective models. The account connects joint attention to shared symbols through the coupling of private inference.

items.title: Modeling the Disjunction Effect within Classical Probability: A New Decision Process Model and Comparison with Quantum-like Models
items.subtitle: ARXIV · Q-BIO.NC · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Ryo Nasu, Yoshihiro Maruyama
items.summary: arXiv:2603.23233v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In a Prisoner's Dilemma experiment, participants defected less often when the opponent's move was unknown than when they were told that the opponent had defected or that the opponent had cooperated. This disjunction effect has often been interpreted as a violation of the classical law of total probability and has motivated quantum-like models of decision making. We re-examine this interpretation and identify a strong assumption implicit in the conventional classical model. The conventional model uses the two informed conditions to represent the full range of participants' expectations and thus treats every participant as certain of the opponent's move even when that move is unknown. We relax this premise by introducing a continuous parameter for each participant's degree of expectation that the opponent will defect. Participants are grouped by expectation level, with the intermediate groups representing ambiguous expectations. A standard quantum-like model offers a different account of this same uncertainty about the opponent's move. In that model, ambiguity arises through superposition, and ambiguous pure states are generic (dense and of full unitarily invariant measure on the unit sphere), so certainty states are mathematically exceptional. Despite this difference in how ambiguity is represented, the proposed classical model can reproduce the observed strong disjunction effect while satisfying the classical law of total probability. More generally, we prove that it can exactly reproduce any triple of defection rates strictly between zero and one, including every such triple generated by the quantum-like model. The proposed model is therefore no less expressive than the quantum-like model for these three observable rates while remaining entirely within classical probability, and the substantive difference between the two lies in how they represent ambiguity and interpret events.

items.subtitle: ARXIV · Q-BIO.NC · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Jacob A. Zavatone-Veth
items.summary: arXiv:2606.31944v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Principal component analysis is widely used to characterize structure in the dynamics of recurrent neural networks. For stationary noise-driven dynamics, the distribution of variance among the principal components is determined by the spectrum of the stationary covariance matrix. While the spectral properties of this matrix are well-understood for linear networks with normal synaptic weight matrices, our understanding of the stationary covariance spectrum for random non-normal dynamics remains incomplete. In this note, we use a free-probability approach to show almost-sure convergence of the stationary covariance spectrum of discrete-time dynamics with random non-normal Gaussian weights, and derive a closed functional equation characterizing its distribution. This characterization allows us to analyze the behavior of tail eigenvalues in the critical regime: they decay with the inverse-square of their rank. In contrast, applying the same approach to the analogous continuous-time dynamics leads to an infinite hierarchy of Schwinger-Dyson equations, rather than a closed scalar equation.

items.title: When Can an AI Agent Serve as a Model of Human Psychopathology?
items.subtitle: ARXIV · Q-BIO.NC · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Marc-Andre Schulz, Pauline Scheuber
items.summary: arXiv:2611.28405v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language models and AI agents are increasingly described in psychiatric terms, such as anxious, depressed, addicted or helpless. A recent study even proposed language models as experimental systems for psychiatry and as a platform for piloting psychological treatments. We ask when an experiment on an AI agent can provide evidence about a specified human psychiatric process. A claim to such evidence has three parts. Something changed in the agent, and the agent's history caused the change. Nothing other than a process shared with people explains that change. The change matches one theory of the human process and not that theory's rivals. Psychiatry and its neighbouring fields have an evidence standard for each part, from the diagnostic manuals' rule for induced states, from clinical test scores and from animal models. We translate each standard into a criterion that a machine study can meet. For a language model the most critical alternative to a shared process is extrapolation from its training text, which already contains descriptions of how people respond to trauma and how they answer questionnaires. We show how to probe that alternative. Further, we audited forty-three published studies that apply psychiatric terms to a machine or induce a comparable state in one. Most compared the machine with an identical copy that had not gone through the history that induced the state. None excluded extrapolation from training text. Three tested a psychiatric theory against its rivals, and none of the three tests was conclusive. Until better evidence exists, a treatment pilot on a language model is best read as the model's forecast of patient response, and not as an experiment on a model organism. Evidence for a model organism will come from states induced by what happens to the machine, from experiments on its internal workings, and from tests on which rival theories disagree.

items.title: Simulating Episodic Like Memory in Octopus: Breaking the Rules
items.subtitle: ARXIV · Q-BIO.NC · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Jeffrey L. Krichmar
items.summary: arXiv:2611.28409v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Episodic memory, which involves the recollection of past events, has been observed in several species including the invertebrate cuttlefish. In a subsequent experiment, episodic memory was not observed in the closely related octopus. Rather the octopus used simpler, cognitive rule-based strategies to gain access to food. Using a prior model of cuttlefish episodic-like memory, we replicated the octopus experiment. Under less challenging conditions, episodic memory and the simpler cognitive strategies all had positive gains. However, under more challenging conditions, which introduced the threat of predation, only the episodic memory model had positive gains. These results suggest that if challenged ecologically, it would be advantageous for octopus to use episodic-like memory. We discuss possible reasons for the behavioral discrepancies in these closely related cephalopods.

items.subtitle: ARXIV · Q-BIO.NC · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Weiheng Yao, Changhong Jing, Xuhang Chen, Chi-Man Pun, Michael Kwok-Po Ng, Shuqiang Wang
items.summary: arXiv:2611.28507v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Electrophysiological and haemodynamic recordings resolve brain activity at complementary temporal and spatial scales, yet paired acquisition remains difficult to scale. We propose a generative framework that aligns paired multimodal recordings in a unified representation space and generates modality-specific haemodynamic responses from EEG. In paired cohorts, the framework generated fMRI BOLD and fNIRS haemoglobin responses that reproduced regional dynamics, cortical maps, functional connectivity and task structure. Generated BOLD followed Real BOLD time courses and cortical patterns, while Generated haemoglobin responses tracked task-evoked HbO and HbR dynamics. The framework enabled decoding across visual, motor-imagery and mental-arithmetic tasks, independent-record decoding, external BOLD localization and low-sample augmentation. Paired feature-space calibration supported bidirectional retrieval. The proposed framework extends cortical analysis and brain decoding to EEG recordings when Real haemodynamic data are sparse.

items.title: Scaling of phase rigidity without eigenstate coalescence
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Shang-En Xie, Li-Mei Chen, Yao Zhou, Peng Ye
items.summary: arXiv:2611.29463v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Phase rigidity vanishes as a power law near exceptional points, reflecting the coalescence of eigenstates at these points. In this Letter, we show that non-Hermitian skin effects induce distinct asymptotic behaviors of phase rigidity without eigenstate coalescence. To demonstrate this, we derive exact analytical results for three non-Hermitian chain models and verify them numerically. For the ordinary skin effect, phase rigidity decays exponentially with increasing system size $N$, as the right and left eigenstates are exponentially localized at opposite boundaries. For the scale-free skin effect, phase rigidity exhibits an $N^{-2}$ power-law approach to a nonzero constant as the right and left eigenstates have decay lengths proportional to $N$. For the algebraic skin effect studied here, phase rigidity can exhibit an $N^{-1/2}$ power-law decay to zero, with the right eigenstate algebraically localized near a boundary and the left eigenstate spread across the chain. These findings show that non-Hermitian skin effects govern phase-rigidity scaling by shaping the spatial profiles of the right and left eigenstates, enabling control of eigenstate nonorthogonality without exceptional points.

items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Jack Mandell (Department of Mathematical Sciences, Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute), Adam Leicester (Department of Materials Science and Engineering, Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute), Zixu Wang (Department of Materials Science and Engineering, Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute), Jian Shi (Department of Materials Science and Engineering, Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute, Department of Physics, Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute), Haimeng Zhang (IBM Quantum, IBM T.J. items.summary: arXiv:2611.29019v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Structure-aware optimizers have been the focus of recent study for the optimization of parameters in variational quantum circuits. Many of these optimizers follow a coordinate-based paradigm, making single parameter updates by using classical approximations to the cost function generated from quantum sampling. However, the performance of structure-aware optimizers on real quantum hardware at large system size has yet to be demonstrated. Recently, Interpolation-based Coordinate Descent (ICD) has been proposed to unify many of these optimizers into one framework. ICD requires a preset frequency set for interpolation, which can be theoretically derived, but for which the cost function is generally sparse over and may require manual tuning. To address these issues, we propose Frequency-learning Interpolation-based Coordinate Descent (FLICD) to adaptively learn frequencies online, allowing easier scaling up to larger systems. We demonstrate that our algorithm is more accurate than an existing zeroth-order method COBYLA and requires fewer quantum resources than ICD on simulator. Using IBM quantum hardware, we execute FLICD on systems up to 100 qubits and observe robust performance with an increasing number of layers.

items.author: Mirela Selimovi\'{c}, Josip Bajo, Mikl\'{o}s Horv\'{a}th, Juan Jos\'e Romero, Thomas Heine, Philip Walther, Rupert Ursin, Sebastian Philipp Neumann
items.summary: arXiv:2611.29046v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a robust, compact polarization-entangled photon-pair source based on bulk optics that achieves long-term stability, a spectral pair generation rate of $4.24 \times 10^6$ pairs s$^{-1}$ mW$^{-1}$ nm$^{-1}$ constant for pump powers up to 700 mW, an intrinsic heralding efficiency of 59.8% , and a polarization contrast visibility of 99.6%. items.title: Single-Phonon-Gated Pair Charging of Quantum Batteries
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Xiaolong Zhao, Yazhuang Miao, Shuo Liang, Tianhui Qiu, Libin Fu
items.summary: arXiv:2611.29130v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Charging a quantum battery requires both an energy source and access to a channel through which that energy can be transferred. If that access depends on a quantum state, charging becomes conditional on the state while the external controls remain unchanged. We show that a single phonon in a common mechanical mode enables a second-order resonant pair transition in a two-cell battery formed by the electronic spins of two nitrogen-vacancy centers, whereas the mechanical vacuum supports no corresponding resonance. At fixed controls and mean phonon number, the final stored energy and ergotropy reached with a one-phonon Fock state are unattainable with any classical mixture of coherent states. An energy balance shows that the microwave drives supply nearly all of the stored energy, while the phonon contributes only a small fraction. Our results open a route to quantum-state-conditioned charging in quantum batteries under experimentally feasible parameters.

items.title: Undecidable quantum storage: no algorithm can tell from the noise rate whether a fixed circuit remembers
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Seth Douglas, Nidhal Mghirbi
items.summary: arXiv:2611.29134v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Below a threshold noise rate, error correction lets larger quantum memories store a qubit for longer, without limit. Can the noise rate alone tell us whether a given noisy circuit does this? We construct fixed local circuits for which no algorithm can, already in one dimension under single-qubit noise. Each circuit is translation-invariant and time-periodic, with depolarizing noise on every wire after every layer, including all classical control. A computable list of disjoint rate intervals is indexed by the inputs $n$ of a universal Turing machine; local noise statistics select the input that the circuit simulates, and halting triggers erasure. If the machine runs forever on $n$, a qubit is stored throughout the $n$-th interval at entanglement fidelity at least $15/16$ for a time that grows without bound with size: linearly on rings, exponentially in six dimensions. The encoding and decoding maps are noiseless and global; they depend on $n$, the system size and, for decoding, the time, but not on the rate. If it halts, the fidelity of every encoding falls below $1/2+\eta$, for any fixed $\eta>0$, after a time independent of size and rate. The labels of the intervals with unbounded storage form a $\Pi^0_1$-complete set, and intervals of both kinds accumulate at zero, so these circuits have no noise threshold. Without rate selection, the ring construction is a translation-invariant, time-periodic memory: from an initialized classical hierarchy it stores a qubit for a time linear in the ring length at every sufficiently small rate, addressing the memory part of a one-dimensional question raised by D\"unnweber, Styliaris and Trivedi. These are existence results: registers and interaction ranges are very large and the rates astronomically small.

items.title: Where to Hide the Traps: Robust Placement in Verifiable Blind Quantum Computation
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Noureldin Mohamed, Saif Al-Kuwari
items.summary: arXiv:2611.29258v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Trap-based verification of blind quantum computation hides test qubits among the positions of a measurement pattern, and existing protocols choose the trap configuration without regard to the delegated computation. We model trap placement as a zero-sum game between a client, who chooses a trap distribution, and a server, who chooses where to apply a Pauli deviation, with a damage profile $w$ and a per-trap detection constant $c$. Since the client cannot know how damage from several positions combines, we solve the game for all monotone subadditive damage functions consistent with $w$ at once. In a single round, placing traps in proportion to $w$ guarantees soundness error $1-c/\|w\|_1$ and is optimal up to a factor $1+\max_iw_i$, while the optimistic solution can fail completely. Over $T$ test rounds, the error decays exponentially against a server that repeats the same deviation, but a general server can keep it at $\Theta(\|w\|_1/(cT))$, and against such servers the damage-weighted placement is exactly optimal. Damage profiles follow from the flow of the pattern: for brickwork patterns with $m=4h+1$ columns, only $(2h+1)^2$ positions can affect a decision qubit, whatever the width. With $k$ traps per round, placing them on this set reduces the number of test rounds by the same factor as for a single trap; with unrestricted trap sets and flat damage we recover the known optimality of fractional coloring. Finally, trap statistics certify the aggregate damage with a number of rounds independent of the number of positions $N$, whereas locating the damage requires $\Omega(N\epsilon^{-2}\log\delta^{-1})$ rounds.

items.title: Quantum Geometric Tensor in Parameter-Dependent Quasi-Hermitian Systems
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Ming-Zhang Wang, Xu-Yang Hou, Hao Guo
items.summary: arXiv:2611.29314v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A parameter-dependent physical inner product makes the comparison of quantum states at different parameter points non-unique. We formulate two geometric prescriptions for this comparison in quasi-Hermitian systems. The Type I QGT is defined by an inner-product-compatible covariant derivative and horizontal projection. It is a Hermitian, positive-semidefinite Gram tensor, and, for any normalized solution of the inner-product-preserving dynamics, its tangential component equals the physical energy variance. The Type II QGT is constructed from the endpoint overlap of physical dual states and is invariant under local $GL(1,\mathbb{C})$ rescalings. We show that, on a normalized section, it coincides with the established left--right (LR) QGT, while providing an endpoint-overlap interpretation of that tensor. Our central result is an exact relation between the two constructions: in the positive Dyson frame, the Type I QGT is the positive Gram block of the dressed-derivative sector, while the real symmetric part of the Type II QGT is this metric minus a positive-semidefinite contribution from the metric connection; the full complex tensor also contains cross terms. This relation clarifies the origin of the possible indefiniteness of the Type II metric and separates it from the positivity of the physical Hilbert-space metric. We further distinguish instantaneous Dyson mappings from the fixed inner-product-preserving dynamics and characterize the conditions under which the corresponding QGTs agree. Three two-level models illustrate these results. The physical content of the two tensors is then identified through the energy uncertainty and evolution speed for Type I, and the symmetrized endpoint overlap, complex holonomy, and signed dynamical response for Type II.

items.title: Approximation of Semigroups of Random Processes on a Hilbert Space
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: A. V. Utkin
items.summary: arXiv:2611.29359v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper develops Chernoff-type approximation methods for strongly continuous and bi-continuous semigroups of operators arising in the stochastic dynamics of quantum systems. The main focus is on applying Chernoff iterations to Markov semigroups of multiplicative random processes on separable infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces. The justification of the passage from discrete quantum measurements to continuous ones depends essentially on the choice of topology and function spaces. We propose conditions for convergence to bi-continuous semigroups on subspaces that weaken the classical requirements of the Chernoff theorem. The existence of the limiting bi-continuous semigroup is established in each of the three cases: commutation of the approximating operators, their asymptotic commutation, and uniform convergence of difference quotients over a family of approximating operators. For diffusive models with a generator having bounded coefficients, the derivative of the approximating function is computed explicitly on the subspace of test functions with rapidly decreasing second derivative; the limitations of applicability of this result are discussed. Applications to generalized models of continuous imprecise quantum measurement with unbounded observables, as well as to Poisson and diffusion processes, are outlined as directions for further research.

items.title: Optimizer or physics? Machine-learning surrogates for collision-based preparation of multipartite entangled quantum states
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Duc-Kha Vu, Minh Tam Nguyen, \"Ozg\"ur E. M\"ustacapl{\i}o\u{g}lu, Fatih Ozaydin
items.summary: arXiv:2611.29384v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Repeated partial-SWAP collisions can prepare symmetric Dicke states, including the $W$ state, without measurement or postselection. The collision sequence uses only two global collision angles, and its fidelity is evaluated after a final layer of local phase rotations is optimized numerically, so each candidate pair requires a many-qubit simulation and a phase fit. We study when learned surrogates reduce the number of such evaluations, and what limits the best-found fidelity, for 65 Dicke targets with 11--20 qubits in noiseless simulations. At 50 evaluations per target, Gaussian-process Bayesian optimization (GP-BO) exceeds fixed Sobol and grid designs by 0.088 and 0.063 in mean best-found fidelity. Bounded Nelder--Mead reaches 0.760 against 0.762 for GP-BO, and has the higher three-seed mean on 41 of the 61 targets with a reference value; in this two-parameter problem, adaptivity matters far more than the choice between the two methods. A neural-network ensemble pretrained on 750 observations from smaller systems needs 32\% fewer new evaluations per target than GP-BO at comparable fidelity, but the full neural search takes 1.6 times the wall time of GP-BO in our implementation. In a separate source-only test, the best of five neural proposals per target exceeds the best of five population-model proposals by 0.070 in mean fidelity. Exact symmetries and state diagnostics help explain why the leading adaptive methods reach similar family-mean fidelities. The collisions conserve the magnitude of the bare Dicke overlap and the total-spin weights, and for the best controls on a 12-target diagnostic panel, 79% of the infidelity is an amplitude deficit that a final phase layer cannot remove, which motivates interleaved phase control.

items.title: Bogoliubov-picture thermofield dynamics in anharmonic environments
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Rocco Martinazzo, Bartosz B{\l}asiak, Irene Burghardt
items.summary: arXiv:2611.29427v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Thermofield dynamics (TFD) describes finite-temperature quantum relaxation through a purified wavefunction, without sampling thermally populated initial states. For harmonic environments, TFD is typically combined with a thermal Bogoliubov transformation to obtain a compact wavefunction representation. This transformation can also be useful for anharmonic baths, but preparing the corresponding thermal state in the transformed representation poses additional numerical challenges. Here, we explore TFD approaches tailored to anharmonic potentials and compatible with efficient tensor network methods for quantum propagation. We show that the conceptually appealing route of converting a harmonic-reference thermal state into the target anharmonic state by imaginary-time propagation can be numerically ill-conditioned. As a practical alternative, we formulate a multilayer multiconfiguration time-dependent Hartree (ML-MCTDH) protocol that separates thermal-state preparation from the harmonic-reference Bogoliubov transformation. We prepare the thermal purification in the bare representation and then apply finite-basis Bogoliubov unitaries to the physical--auxiliary mode pairs. For independent bath modes, direct construction of the thermal amplitude provides a complementary initialization procedure. We illustrate this protocol through vibrational relaxation and spatial-superposition decoherence of a harmonic subsystem coupled to a Morse-oscillator bath. We find non-monotonic energy relaxation, shifts in the dominant resonant response, and oscillatory energy exchange at zero and finite temperature. For decoherence, we recover the expected harmonic-bath scaling and find a pronounced non-monotonic dependence of the decay rate on anharmonicity at finite temperature in a low-frequency model, with a weaker dependence in a high-frequency model.

items.title: No-Go Theorems for Transversal and Automorphism Clifford Gates on Prime-Dimensional Qudit Stabilizer Codes
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Yuchen Zhan, Qi Ye, Dong-Ling Deng
items.summary: arXiv:2611.29430v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Logical Clifford gates are a basic primitive of fault-tolerant quantum computation. For stabilizer codes on qudits of prime dimension $p$ that encode $k\geq 2$ logical qudits, we prove that Clifford gadgets that are transversal with respect to a fixed partition of the physical qudits into blocks of fewer than $k$ qudits cannot realize the full logical Clifford group, and that this block size is tight. Code automorphisms, which combine single-qudit Clifford gates with qudit permutations, also fail for every $p$. Both obstructions come from prime-order logical Clifford elements that these gadgets cannot reach.

items.title: Multi-port few-photon diodes
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Teng-Fei Xiao, Liang Li, Renli Xu, Tiantian Li, Junlong Tian, Jinlei Tan, Jie Peng
items.summary: arXiv:2611.29451v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate single- and two-photon scattering dynamics in a system comprising two one dimensional chiral waveguides coupled to a dissipative Rydberg atom pair. By employing the Laplace transform method, we analytically solve the scattering problem and characterize the transport properties. Our results demonstrate robust perfect single-photon diode effects in this system with or without dissipation, exhibiting unity transmittance in the forward direction and zero transmittance in the backward direction. Unlike previous studies where perfect nonreciprocity requires a specific dissipation rate, our scheme achieves this effect without fine-tuning such parameters. Furthermore, we extend the nonreciprocal transport to multi-port configurations at the one and two-photon levels. The system exhibits pronounced photon nonreciprocal behavior in lossy and lossless scenarios, without the need for precise parameter matching. This work provides a robust platform for on-chip nonreciprocal photonic devices.

items.title: Revealing the Hidden Symmetry of the Asymmetric Quantum Rabi Model
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Zi-Min Li, Zi-Cheng Liu, Long-Jie Li, Xuan Zou, Jin-Xiang Fu, Xilin Lu, Murray T. Batchelor
items.summary: arXiv:2611.28677v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A longitudinal bias breaks ordinary parity in the asymmetric quantum Rabi model, yet exact crossings reappear when the bias equals an integer multiple $m$ of the oscillator energy spacing. We trace the hidden symmetry to exchange between equal-energy partners $m$ rungs apart on two displaced oscillator ladders. Tunneling to other rungs makes this exchange vary in time. We construct the exact symmetry operator by adding spin and oscillator coherences that cancel this variation. At nonzero coupling and tunneling, the resulting charge has no zero modes, and its sign divides the full Hilbert space into two generalized-parity sectors that cannot mix. Spin-resolved mirror interference probes coherence between the two opposite-parity states at a crossing. Its small-displacement exponent gives $m$, and its leading coefficient, together with the charge magnitude, predicts the mixing induced by a slight change in bias.

items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Adam Rutkowski
items.summary: arXiv:2611.28700v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Decomposable positive maps cannot detect entangled states with positive partial transpose (PPT). We obtain a necessary and sufficient criterion for decomposability in the entire seven-real-parameter class of Hermiticity-preserving cyclic-sign covariant maps on $M_3$. items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Borhan Ahmadi
items.summary: arXiv:2611.28738v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study an interacting quantum-battery chain in which a synthetic flux controls interference between hopping paths. Keeping the internal battery Hamiltonian fixed, we seek the flux that leaves the most extractable work. Even a Gaussian reconstruction supplied with exact one-body information can rank competing flux settings incorrectly. A reduced many-body model that retains correlations within a few battery-occupation sectors recovers the correct ranking and selects nearly optimal fluxes across the finite systems and parameter ranges studied. Strikingly, the model can make an accurate control choice even when it excludes configurations carrying substantial probability in the exact state. Thus, choosing a nearly optimal charging flux can require much less information than reconstructing the full many-body state.

items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Komal Kumar, Shree Prakash
items.summary: arXiv:2611.28749v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Purity quantifies quantum-state mixedness, motivating the study of its role in controlling entropy variations. A sharp purity-based continuity bound is established for the von Neumann entropy of qubit states. The bound is attainable for every admissible purity difference and strictly improves the existing purity bound. In higher dimensions, an explicit sharp bound is derived within the family of pure states mixed with the maximally mixed state. Further continuity estimates are obtained for conditional entropy, quantum mutual information, quantum conditional mutual information, and squashed entanglement within specified bipartite and tripartite families. An application to machine learning assisted qubit entropy estimation illustrates how the sharp bound converts purity estimation errors into rigorous entropy error bounds.

items.title: Quantum Metrology With Quantum Limit Cycles
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Zhi-Hao Liu, Xiangyu Niu, Keren Li, Ran Liu, Xiao-Dong Yang, Jun Li
items.summary: arXiv:2611.28801v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Beyond nonclassical states, emergent quantum phenomena offer new metrological resources. Quantum limit cycles, in particular, sustain long-lived oscillations that prolong coherent signal accumulation. However, quantum fluctuations may limit this advantage, leaving their metrological performance unclear. Here, we propose a quantum limit-cycle metrology protocol for collective spins by introducing nonlinear damping into the conventional collective-decay protocol. We develop a semiclassical phase-diffusion theory to characterize its metrological performance, in good agreement with numerical simulations. The limit-cycle protocol improves estimation precision and approaches Heisenberg scaling with system size. We further combine limit-cycle dynamics with spin squeezing, finding that squeezing improves short-time precision, but phase diffusion ultimately dominates, leaving the asymptotic scaling unchanged. Our results establish quantum limit cycles as a metrological resource and clarify the interplay between limit-cycle dynamics and squeezing in quantum sensing.

items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Baichu Yu, Zhang Zhou, Zhiyuan Li, Jiajun Zhang
items.summary: arXiv:2611.28837v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The accessible information of a quantum ensemble can be strictly smaller than its Holevo information because a single-copy measurement may discard part of the label--system correlation. We ask whether information represented across two alternative measurement contexts can bridge this gap without assigning a joint distribution to their outcomes. Building on the relative-entropy-based projection method introduced by Harder et al., we define the directed posterior novelty of each record relative to the other, and an associated total-information quantity. For posterior-orthogonal records, this quantity equals the sum of the two record mutual informations. For finite-dimensional classical--quantum ensembles, we prove that optimizing this quantity over pairs of POVMs yields a value between the accessible and Holevo information. The upper bound follows by showing that the directed posterior novelty provides a lower bound on the infimum of the measured-relative-entropy recovery error. The uniform BB84 ensemble provides an example in which the quantity saturates the Holevo information while strictly exceeding the accessible information. Finally, we analytically establish the quantum validity of a redundancy-based information causality condition, resolving a question that has remained open since the condition was introduced.

items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Kenta Kasai
items.summary: arXiv:2611.28847v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give an explicit construction of quantum low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes without searching for candidates at each size. A fixed pair partition (PP) and fixed integer parameters determine the parity-check matrices at a specified size. Using affine permutation matrices (APMs), we construct a $[[3072,772,32]]$ code with column weight 3 and check weight 8 in each of the X and Z parity-check matrices. A construction based on circulant permutation matrices (CPMs) gives $[[1270,260,\ge34]]$, with column weight 4 and check weight 10. We prove that the construction yields commuting checks and verify the resulting distances using exhaustive search and logical operators. For the main construction, we conjecture the existence of a finite structural distance upper bound and distance improvement toward that bound as the size increases.

items.title: The resource--invariant gap: a protected Floquet invariant need not protect Wigner negativity
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Juste Deuyekbe, Philippe Djorw\'e, Nsangou Mama, S. G. Nana Engo
items.summary: arXiv:2611.28904v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Topological invariants constrain a driven Floquet generator, yet whether they protect a transient nonlinear bosonic resource remains open. We track boundary Wigner negativity of an even cat state in a chiral Floquet Su--Schrieffer--Heeger chain with boundary Kerr nonlinearity and structured loss. The quasienergy windings remain quantized at every chain length, yet the matched sector contrast flips sign when the chain grows under index-end shielding and is null within $3\times 10^{-5}$ under uniform loss at $t=T$ for $d\le 0.5$. Prepared and shielded on the physical dangling end, the contrast remains positive, modulated by local dimer return rather than set by the invariant. A three-site causal light cone and a boundary-Laplacian erosion law trace the flip to strong-bond bulk exposure: the sign is set by where the bulk-rate loss sits relative to the prepared site, not by chain length. We call this decoupling the resource--invariant gap.

items.title: Long-time dynamics of open quantum systems: mathematical and physical aspects
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Daniele Amato, Paolo Facchi, Giovanni Gramegna, Arturo Konderak
items.summary: arXiv:2611.28906v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum channels provide the mathematical framework for describing the evolution of open quantum systems, i.e., quantum systems interacting with an environment. This review focuses on the long-time or asymptotic dynamics of open quantum systems, a topic of growing interest due to its relevance for quantum information theory and noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices. We present a comprehensive analysis of homogeneous evolutions in both discrete and continuous time, treating the dynamics in full generality within the Schr\"odinger and Heisenberg pictures. By systematically studying the spectral properties of quantum channels, we present general structure theorems that characterize asymptotic behaviour, illustrated through several paradigmatic examples. We further discuss how the asymptotic dynamics can be exploited for dissipative state engineering, the identification of decoherence-free subspaces, the design of quantum error-correction schemes, and the evaluation of the asymptotic capacities of quantum channels.

items.title: Non-Abelian Twist Defects in Bivariate Bicycle Codes
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Rui Zeng, Li-Wei Yu
items.summary: arXiv:2611.28944v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Bivariate bicycle quantum low-density parity-check codes combine efficient quantum storage with a rich Abelian anyon structure, providing a compelling platform for exploring the interplay between quantum error correction and topological order. A central challenge is how to realize domain walls that host non-Abelian twist defects at their endpoints. Here we explicitly construct electric-magnetic duality walls for arbitrary bivariate bicycle codes with finite anyon content using composite, interblock, and patch checks. These checks remove the unwanted local modes while preserving charge conversion, ensuring that topologically contractible closed ribbons act trivially on encoded states. For each fixed code, check weights and interaction ranges remain bounded independently of wall length. The wall endpoints have quantum dimension $2^{Q/2}$, where $Q$ counts the independent generators in each electric or magnetic charge space. As an application, we illustrate measurement-only braiding for $Q=3$ under the correspondence between measurements and defect transport. Our construction provides a valuable basis for exploring non-Abelian defect physics and developing logical operations in quantum low-density parity-check codes with Abelian topological order in future.

items.title: Q-TRACE: Physics-based zero-day attack detection for decoy-state quantum key distribution
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Sumit Tapas Chongder (Indian Institute of Technology Jodhpur, Jodhpur, India)
items.summary: arXiv:2611.28945v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Practical quantum key distribution (QKD) is secure only while its devices match the assumptions of the security proof, and implementation attacks exploit mismatches while keeping the quantum bit error rate (QBER) low. We formulate attack detection in decoy-state BB84 as a sequential test against the honest-device manifold, the set of receiver statistics an attack-free link can produce under arbitrary channel loss. The resulting monitor, Q-TRACE (Quantum Telemetry Residuals Against Calibrated Expectations), calibrates a physical model of each link on commissioning data, profiles out the transmittance, and combines omnibus residual, physics score and setting-allocation tests with drift-robust references; no attack data are used. The formulation also yields a detectability exponent D* that lower-bounds the delay of any telemetry monitor and vanishes for a Trojan-horse probe with filtered back-reflection. On a count-level twin with model mismatch, over five held-out seeds and at a per-window false-alarm rate of 10^-3, Q-TRACE detects 63.6% of links under known attacks, 28.0% under unseen attack families and 65.3% under composite attacks, versus at most 51.2%, 6.7% and 42.3% for industry monitors, unsupervised and quantum-kernel detectors and a supervised classifier. Its delay attains the bound for strongly detectable attacks. On 33 parallel BB84 links of the IBM Heron processor ibm_marrakesh with physically executed entangling and amplitude-damping eavesdroppers, the measured information-disturbance relations agree with theory; a commissioning reference acquired under different operating conditions triggers alarms in every monitor tested, while a condition-matched reference detects a probe with 0.3% ideal QBER increase on 14 of 14 link-epochs with no false alarm on 66 honest ones.

items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: A. I. Komech, E. A. Kopylova
items.summary: arXiv:2611.28962v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider damped driven version of the Jaynes-Cummings equation which describes quantised one-mode Maxwell field coupled to a two-level molecule. The pumping and dissipation operator are polynomial in the creation and annihilation operators. The structure of the dissipation operator corresponds to the theory of completely positive trace preserving operators due to Lindblad, Kossakowski and others. We construct examples of {\it locked states} which are stationary states of the corresponding averaged dynamics in the interaction picture. The states are nonnegative Hermitian density operators with finite Hilbert-Schmidt norm. The calculations rely on the recurrence equation for diagonal entries.

We then construct infinite families of trees admitting perfect state transfer, disproving their conjecture in the general case.

items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Lasse H. Wolff, Matthias Christandl, Bergfinnur Durhuus, Christoph Hirche, Andreas Winter
items.summary: arXiv:2611.28361v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For a small classical system correlated with a large one, it is always possible to compress the large system down to a size only dependent on the size of the smaller one, while preserving all correlations up to a given controllable error. Here, we show that such a statement does not hold at all when the large system is quantum mechanical. More precisely, we show that there are bipartite states such that any compression of the large system, by a non-trivial relative factor, will necessarily lead to the destruction of a significant amount of correlation, measured in mutual information. Our results therefore identify a limitation of information-bottleneck approaches to quantum machine learning, showing that a small system specifying the relevant features contained in a large quantum data set does not guarantee a compact encoding of the latter that preserves the relevant correlations.

items.title: Online Scheduling for Entanglement Distillation: Learning When to Wait
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Panagiotis Promponas, Spyros Tserkis, Leandros Tassiulas
items.summary: arXiv:2611.28373v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Entanglement distillation probabilistically increases the fidelity of entangled pairs at the cost of reducing their number. The outcome of each distillation operation takes time to communicate, during which the entangled pairs decohere while idle in their memories. This raises a dilemma: wait for the outcome before proceeding, or continue optimistically at the risk of needlessly consuming further pairs. We study online distillation scheduling, in which distillation trees are constructed dynamically to maximize the throughput of pairs that meet a required fidelity. A policy decides which pairs to distill together and, for each operation, whether to wait for its outcome. We derive an upper bound on the throughput of every scheduling policy and, by formulating the problem as a Markov decision process, train, with reinforcement learning, a policy that applies to any number of memories. Compared with two baselines that always or never wait, the learned policy delivers as many pairs of the required fidelity as the better one when one of these two extremes is the best choice, and more otherwise.

items.title: Verification and Evaluation of A Comprehensive Quantum Simulation Compiler
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Bhuwan Joshi, Zoukarneini Difaizi Tagba, Zhi Xiang Chong, Liyi Li
items.summary: arXiv:2611.28388v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hamiltonian simulation is a central application of quantum computing, yet most existing compilers offer no machine-checked guarantee that the circuits they produce approximate the intended evolution. The previous QBlue compiler verifies a Hamiltonian simulation compiler containing only Trotter-based algorithms. It takes a Hamiltonian written over Pauli strings, a simulation time, and an error bound, and produces a circuit or analog schedule that is proven, in the Rocq proof assistant, to approximate the ideal time evolution within that bound and proves a single end-to-end error bound that composes the errors of the individual stages; the compiler uses it to select, by resource estimation, the cheapest algorithm that meets the user's bound. This paper advances the verification efforts with two further steps. First, we extend QBlue to $\textsf{QBlue}_{\texttt{BE}}$ by verifying another important compilation method for Hamiltonian simulation: block-encoding-based (BE-based) algorithms. Second, we empirically evaluate 279 Hamiltonian simulation programs against the state-of-the-art BE-based compiler, PennyLane. For many programs, our compiler shows a $94\%$ gate reduction compared to PennyLane. Additionally, we also discover issues and bugs in PennyLane. We also compare Trotter- and BE-based algorithms, providing a practical comparison for the long-standing debate over which algorithms perform better. Our results surprisingly show that Trotter-based algorithms may gain a practical advantage, even though BE algorithms have a theoretical advantage.

items.title: Froq: Safe Speculative Execution on Live Quantum States for FTQC
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Yicheng Guang, Yueqi Chen
items.summary: arXiv:2611.28427v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reducing execution time is critical to fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) as longer executions expose logical qubits to more opportunities for failure. However, quantum processors could frequently stall due to slow classical error-correction decoders. Recent speculative decoding accelerates this process, but its speculation remains on the classical side, leaving quantum operations waiting for confirmed decoding results. Extending speculative execution to the quantum side is fundamentally challenging. Unlike classical processor states, quantum states cannot be arbitrarily copied or checkpointed for rollback, making recovery from mispredictions difficult. In this work, we propose Froq to enable safe speculative execution on live quantum states. Froq uses compiler-assisted recovery contracts to track how mispredictions propagate through quantum operations. It further employs a resource-aware runtime mechanism to reserve recovery workspace and dynamically balance the benefits of speculative execution against the expected costs of recovery. We evaluate Froq on eight FTQC programs across 88 configurations, building on an existing speculative window decoder. Froq reduces quantum-side time by 9.81% across all 88 configurations. The reduction reaches 18.34% across the 45 configurations allowing concurrent predictions, and peaks at 31.1% at code distance d=21, under limited resources.
